Small Samples, Big Claims: Re-reading Field Experiments

Abstract

We re-read forty field experiments and find that most were too small to detect the effects they report. Reported effects shrink by about half when the studies are repeated with larger samples.

Introduction

Field experiments have become the default way to test policy ideas. A typical study randomizes a few hundred households and reports an effect of ten percent or more. We ask how often such a study could have found an effect of that size if the true effect were smaller.

The short answer is: rarely. For the median study in our sample, statistical power to detect a five percent effect is below one in four.
